facts.one_liner: Sea stacks, driftwood and misty light on Washington’s wild Pacific coast.
facts.why_go: Ruby Beach, in Olympic National Park, is a moody Pacific beach of sea stacks, giant drift logs and tide pools, with Abbey Island just offshore. Named for its ruby-coloured garnet crystals in the sand, it glows at sunset.
facts.best_time: June–September for drier weather; low tide for tide pools.
facts.how_to_get_there: On US-101 on the Olympic Peninsula, about 3.5 hours’ drive from Seattle.
facts.good_to_know: Swimming is unsafe; watch for rolling logs in the surf.

facts.one_liner: A wide crescent bay beneath waterfall-streaked green mountains on Kauaʻi’s North Shore.
facts.why_go: Hanalei Bay is a two-mile crescent of sand on Kauaʻi’s North Shore, framed by emerald mountains streaked with waterfalls after rain. The historic Hanalei Pier is a local landmark, and the bay is calm for swimming in summer while winter brings big surf.
facts.best_time: May–September for calm water; winter for watching surf.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour’s drive north of Līhuʻe Airport.
facts.good_to_know: Heed lifeguards in winter. Hanalei town has great food trucks.

facts.one_liner: One of the world’s rare green-sand beaches, coloured by olivine crystals.
facts.why_go: Papakōlea, near Ka Lae (South Point) on Hawaiʻi’s Big Island, is one of only a handful of green-sand beaches in the world. Its sand is coloured by olivine eroded from an ancient cinder cone that encloses the bay.
facts.best_time: Year-round; mornings are cooler for the walk.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1.5 hours’ drive from Kona or Hilo, then a hike of about 2.5 miles each way along the coast.
facts.good_to_know: Bring water and sun protection—there is no shade. Taking sand is prohibited.

facts.one_liner: Jet-black volcanic sand where green sea turtles bask.
facts.why_go: Punaluʻu on the Big Island’s southern coast is a beach of black sand formed from lava fragments, fringed by coconut palms. Endangered Hawaiian green sea turtles often rest on the sand, and freshwater springs bubble up into the bay.
facts.best_time: Year-round; mornings for turtles and calm water.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour’s drive from Hawaiʻi Volcanoes National Park.
facts.good_to_know: Keep a respectful distance from turtles. Do not take the black sand.

facts.one_liner: A heart-shaped bay of calm turquoise water on St. Thomas.
facts.why_go: Magens Bay on the north shore of St. Thomas is a sheltered, heart-shaped bay with a mile of white sand and gentle water. It is a public park managed by the Magens Bay Authority, with an arboretum and views from the Drake’s Seat overlook.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 20 minutes’ drive from Charlotte Amalie.
facts.good_to_know: There is an entry fee. Busy on cruise-ship days.

facts.one_liner: A horseshoe of white sand on the island of Culebra.
facts.why_go: Flamenco Beach on Culebra, a small island off Puerto Rico, is a horseshoe-shaped bay of white sand and clear water, regularly ranked among the world’s best beaches. Rusting tanks left from US Navy training are a reminder of the island’s past.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferry from Ceiba (about 1 hour) or short flights from San Juan to Culebra, then a short taxi.
facts.good_to_know: Ferry tickets sell out on weekends. Snorkel at Carlos Rosario beach nearby.

facts.one_liner: A hidden beach inside a collapsed crater, reached by swimming through a tunnel.
facts.why_go: Playa del Amor, the ‘Hidden Beach’, lies inside a hole open to the sky on one of the Marietas Islands off Puerto Vallarta. Visitors swim or paddle through a short tunnel to reach it. The islands are a national park and a UNESCO biosphere reserve, rich in seabirds like blue-footed boobies.
facts.best_time: November–April for calm seas; whale watching December–March.
facts.how_to_get_there: Licensed tours leave from Punta de Mita and Puerto Vallarta, about 45 minutes by boat.
facts.good_to_know: Access is limited by daily permits; book licensed tours and check current opening days.

facts.one_liner: Rainforest meets white sand in Costa Rica’s best-loved national park.
facts.why_go: Manuel Antonio National Park on Costa Rica’s Pacific coast combines rainforest trails with beautiful white-sand beaches. Monkeys, sloths and iguanas are often seen just steps from the sand.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 3 hours’ drive from San José; Quepos has a small airport.
facts.good_to_know: Park entry is ticketed online and closed on some weekdays—check before you go. Don’t feed the monkeys.

facts.one_liner: Twin coves and a thatched lookout on a boulder in Tayrona’s jungle coast.
facts.why_go: Cabo San Juan del Guía is the most famous beach in Tayrona National Natural Park on Colombia’s Caribbean coast: twin sandy coves separated by a rocky point topped by a thatched hut. Reaching it requires a jungle hike past giant boulders and other beaches.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour’s drive from Santa Marta to El Zaino entrance, then a 2–3-hour hike.
facts.good_to_know: The park closes for a few periods each year for ecological rest—check before going.

facts.one_liner: A natural rock arch and sunset dunes in a remote national park.
facts.why_go: Jericoacoara is a laid-back village of sandy streets inside a national park on Brazil’s north-east coast. Its symbol is Pedra Furada, a natural rock arch on the shore, and crowds gather on the big dune each evening to watch the sunset.
facts.best_time: July–December for wind sports; year-round warmth.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly to Jericoacoara (JJD) or Fortaleza, then a 4x4 transfer across the dunes.
facts.good_to_know: An environmental fee is charged. Visit Pedra Furada at low tide.

facts.one_liner: A long, unspoilt beach of white sand on car-free Ilha Grande.
facts.why_go: Lopes Mendes on Ilha Grande, off the coast of Rio de Janeiro state, is a long, unspoilt beach of fine white sand framed by Atlantic Forest. There are no roads on the island—you reach it by boat and a short jungle walk.
facts.best_time: December–April for summer; quieter in shoulder seasons.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferries from Conceição de Jacareí or Angra dos Reis to Abraão, then a boat and short trail.
facts.good_to_know: Bring food and water—facilities are minimal.

facts.one_liner: A perfect curve of white sand framed by pink granite peaks.
facts.why_go: Wineglass Bay in Freycinet National Park on Tasmania’s east coast is a perfect crescent of white sand and blue water, framed by the pink granite peaks of the Hazards. The climb to the lookout is one of Australia’s most popular walks.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 2.5 hours’ drive from Hobart or Launceston.
facts.good_to_know: Park passes are required. The lookout walk takes about 1–1.5 hours return.

facts.one_liner: Sunset camel trains walk 22 km of white sand on the Indian Ocean.
facts.why_go: Cable Beach in Broome stretches for about 22 kilometres of white sand along the Indian Ocean. Its famous sunset camel rides and turquoise water make it one of Australia’s best-known beaches. It takes its name from the telegraph cable laid from Broome to Java in 1889.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly to Broome; the beach is about 10 minutes from town.
facts.good_to_know: Box jellyfish appear November–April—swim in stinger season with care.

facts.one_liner: Brilliant white sand and kangaroos on the beach.
facts.why_go: Lucky Bay in Cape Le Grand National Park near Esperance has some of the whitest sand in Australia and turquoise water. Kangaroos often lounge on the beach, making it a memorable stop on Western Australia’s south coast.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour’s drive east of Esperance.
facts.good_to_know: Park entry fees apply. Don’t feed the kangaroos.

facts.one_liner: Fine quartz sand that squeaks underfoot, flanked by orange granite boulders.
facts.why_go: Squeaky Beach at Wilsons Promontory National Park gets its name from the fine, round quartz grains that squeak when you walk on them. Huge orange-lichen granite boulders frame the bay, and wombats are common around the park.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 3 hours’ drive south-east of Melbourne.
facts.good_to_know: Swimming can be dangerous—check conditions.

facts.one_liner: Norfolk pines, surf and a ferry ride across Sydney Harbour.
facts.why_go: Manly Beach on Sydney’s Northern Beaches is reached by one of the world’s great ferry rides across the harbour. Lined with Norfolk Island pines, it is great for surfing and swimming, with the pedestrian Corso leading back to the ferry wharf.
facts.how_to_get_there: Ferry from Circular Quay takes about 30 minutes.
facts.good_to_know: Swim between the flags. Walk to Shelly Beach for snorkelling.

facts.why_go: Noosa Main Beach is a rare north-facing beach in Queensland, sheltered from big swells and perfect for swimming and learning to surf. Hastings Street’s cafés are steps away, and the coastal walk through Noosa National Park leads to koalas and secluded bays.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 30 minutes’ drive from Sunshine Coast Airport.
facts.good_to_know: Swim between the flags. Parking is limited—use shuttle buses.

facts.why_go: Radhanagar Beach on Swaraj Dweep (Havelock Island) in the Andaman Islands is a long curve of white sand backed by tall tropical forest. Its sunsets are famous, and the clear water is good for swimming.
facts.how_to_get_there: Fly to Port Blair, then a 1.5–2.5-hour ferry to Havelock.
facts.good_to_know: Ferries book out—reserve early.

facts.one_liner: Red laterite cliffs above a sandy beach on Kerala’s coast.
facts.why_go: Varkala in Kerala is unusual for its red laterite cliffs rising straight above the Arabian Sea. Cafés line the clifftop path, and the beach below is also a pilgrimage site, near the Janardhana Swami Temple.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 1 hour by train or road from Thiruvananthapuram.
facts.good_to_know: Currents can be strong. Dress modestly away from the beach.

facts.one_liner: A secret cove of golden sand and palms near Mirissa on Sri Lanka’s south coast.
facts.why_go: Mirissa is a palm-fringed beach town on Sri Lanka’s south coast, famous for whale-watching trips to see blue whales. Its coves, like this ‘Secret Beach’, offer quieter swimming and snorkelling.
facts.best_time: November–April for calm seas and whale watching.
facts.how_to_get_there: About 3 hours’ drive from Colombo via the Southern Expressway; trains stop at nearby Weligama.
facts.good_to_know: Choose responsible whale-watching operators.
